Scientists are reconstructing who they were. | National Geographic 8:35 Dead World Episode 02: Mummies of Fire and Ice HISTORY & CULTURE DEAD WORLD The mummies forged through fire and ice In the second episode of our Dead World series, digital editor Nicholas St. Fleur examines how extreme environments preserved ancient bodies—and how science is revealing their secrets. By Nicholas St. Fleur Published February 23, 2026 In fantasy books and movies, the undead rise from fire and ice. In the real world, mummies can emerge naturally from melting glaciers and dry desert caves. Others were created when bodies were slowly dried in smoke and ash. In this episode of Dead World , our new series about the most fascinating discoveries in archaeology and paleontology, we examine how extreme heat and cold preserved humans and animals for thousands of years. From Ötzi the Iceman locked in an Alpine glacier to smoke-dried human mummies in ancient Asia, desiccated desert cheetahs , and a frozen Siberian wolf cub carrying woolly rhino DNA in its gut, these discoveries reveal lost cultures and extinct animal populations. Through archaeological and genomic research, scientists are reconstructing their ancient lives. Watch the video and let us know what super-dead things we should cover next. This body of work is essential because it moves the discussion beyond simple compliance and suppression costs to focus on net societal benefits. By treating prevention as a strategic investment, this research identifies the most cost-effective interventions for saving lives and reducing property damage. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Firefighters and Archaeologists Collaborate to Protect Historic Mining Site during Monroe Canyon Fire Jun 16, 2026 MONROE, Utah — In early August 2025, a coordinated effort between resource advisors, archaeologists, and wildfire personnel with the BLM, USDA Forest Service, and the now established U.S. Wildland Fire Service sought to protect a historic mining site on Miner’s Ridge from the advancing Monroe Canyon wildfire. The site, dating back to the 1920s, included a collection of wooden structures and mining remnants: three log cabins, a barn-like building, an outhouse, ore stockpiles, two historic debris scatters, and a mining shaft. These features were connected by a network of trails and wagon roads, offering a rare glimpse into Utah’s early mining history. Protecting such vulnerable heritage is why archaeologists are frequently called to active wildfires. Serving as specialized resource advisors, these professionals work directly with Incident Command to identify and map irreplaceable cultural resources before they are lost. But you don’t have to travel to the deep woods or open prairie to experience these otherworldly insects. Your new employer should provide you with a notice of your health coverage options and retirement plan. Consider enrolling in your employer's benefit plans. If your employer offers more than one health plan option – an HMO plan, a preferred provider option, and a fee-for-service plan, for example – compare each to your needs and preferences before making a decision. Ask for copies of two key documents – the Summary Plan Description (SPD) and the Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC) – to get details about covered benefits and costs. Find out what type of plan you have, how it works, and what eligibility requirements you may have to meet. Know what portion of your premium and costs you will pay, how much they will be, and who to talk to if you have questions. Another option to consider is enrolling in coverage through the Health Insurance Marketplace (Marketplace). The Marketplace offers health insurance plans that provide comprehensive health coverage that present their price and benefit information in an SBC so you can make comparisons. Keep in mind that with most job-based health insurance plans, your employer pays part of your premiums. If you pick a Marketplace plan instead, the employer usually doesn’t contribute to your premiums. He is a shopkeeper who lives alongside the busy Dhaka–Chattogram highway in southeastern Bangladesh, where road traffic crashes regularly leave people dead or seriously injured. When a crash happens nearby, he may be among the first to arrive. Sometimes the call comes when he is at home. He finds a rickshaw or a car and rushes to the scene. He treats wounds, reassures frightened victims and contacts their families. If an injury is serious, he helps get the person to hospital. Long after the crash, some of the people he has helped come back to see him. “They tell me and the other volunteers, ‘Your help is unforgettable. We will remember this until our death,’” he says. “I feel happy and proud, I cannot express how much.” Khokon shares that pride with 119 other community first responders trained to improve emergency care for road crash victims through an initiative led by Bangladesh’s Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), with technical support from the World Health Organization (WHO). Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements. The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin. Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said. His grandfather started playing an accordion in cantinas and family parties along the Texas/Mexican border around the late 1800s. Then Flaco's dad, Santiago Jimenez Sr., carried on the family tradition when he released his first record in 1936. Two of the songs you hear Flaco Jimenez play in this Tiny Desk Concert are traditional German polkas; they were popular in the mid-1800s as German immigrants settled in Texas before it became part of the U.S. almost 20 years later. Over time, the two-step stayed the same, but the German lyrics were replaced by the Mexican storytelling song form known as corridos. pages.description: Most dengue infections cause mild flu-like symptoms or no symptoms at all. But at least one person has died from this year’s outbreak in Florida, where health experts worry the disease will become more common in the future
pages.text: Florida Is Facing Its Worst Dengue Outbreak in Decades, With at Least 524 Locally Acquired Cases. Here's What to Know Skip to main content Dengue is a viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes. Joao Paulo Burini via Getty Images This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue , a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31. That’s the highest number recorded there since the disease returned to the state in 2009 , according to Forbes ’ John Drake. For context, only 62 locally acquired cases were documented in 2025. Most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness . But in early September, a Tampa-area woman named Gay Rabb Small died of dengue on her 80th birthday, after developing a tremor and going to the emergency room, per the New York Times ’ Anemona Hartocollis. Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue. “It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” Eva Harris , an infectious diseases expert at the University of California, Berkeley, tells the Times . “This is so very much of an eye-opener.” Here’s what to know about dengue. What is dengue? Dengue is a viral disease spread by mosquitoes, mainly the species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , which are both present in Florida , among other places. Parents can help children fight flu by getting themselves and their children vaccinated against flu each year. Annual flu vaccination offers the best protection against flu and its potentially serious complications in children. Food Poisoning Symptoms Nov. 24, 2025 Key points Symptoms of food poisoning depend on the type of germ you swallowed. The most common symptoms include diarrhea, stomach pain or cramps, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Severe food poisoning can cause bloody diarrhea, diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days, fever over 102°F, frequent vomiting, and dehydration. Symptoms You can get sick with food poisoning after swallowing certain germs, like Salmonella or E. coli . Your symptoms may vary, depending on the germ you swallowed. Symptoms can range from mild to serious and can last for a few hours or several days. Some germs can make you sick within a few hours after you swallow them. Others may take a few days to make you sick. The most common symptoms of food poisoning are: Diarrhea Stomach pain or cramps Nausea Vomiting Fever If you have diarrhea or vomiting, be sure to drink plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration (not having enough water in your body). Food Safety Basics Mar. 9, 2026 At a glance Food can sometimes contain harmful germs, such as Salmonella and norovirus, that can make you sick. If you eat food containing germs, you can get a foodborne illness (sometimes called food poisoning). Some foods are more likely to contain germs, including raw flour and dough, raw chicken, and raw milk. "Food safety" refers to steps you and others can take to prevent foodborne illness. Overview Foods can sometimes be contaminated with germs that can make you sick. Some examples include Salmonella, norovirus, and Campylobacter. What is food safety? Food safety refers to practices that can reduce your risk of getting food poisoning. This is a significant public health burden that is largely preventable. The FDA Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) is transforming the nation’s food safety system by shifting the focus from responding to foodborne illness to preventing it. Congress enacted FSMA in response to dramatic changes in the global food system and in our understanding of foodborne illness and its consequences, including the realization that preventable foodborne illness is both a significant public health problem and a threat to the economic well-being of the food system. FDA has finalized several rules to implement FSMA, recognizing that ensuring the safety of the food supply is a shared responsibility among many different points in the global supply chain for both human and animal food. The FSMA rules are designed to make clear specific actions that must be taken at each of these points to prevent contamination. A coach rumbles past and, for a fleeting moment, I feel a pang of envy for the air-conditioned cocoon its passengers are almost certainly enjoying. Then I look around. From behind tinted windows, they’re missing the street theatre playing out around us. “Cycling is the best way to really see Luxor,” Sayed Setouhy calls over his shoulder, his crown of cropped black curls silhouetted against the sun. “You have the freedom to stop, take pictures and discover things that people in cars and coaches don’t.” It’s morning in Luxor and the city on the banks of the Nile is limbering up for the day. Designed by Hiroshi Sugimoto , even this entryway to the newly renovated Hirshhorn Sculpture Garden is a work of art. “You’ll notice that the distortion kind of changes levels,” says the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden ’s acting head curator Marina Isgro . “It’s sort of at adult-height here, and then as you walk in, it kind of becomes child-height. Sugimoto is really welcoming visitors of all sizes to play with their reflections here in this space.” As we continue the journey into the sunken garden, we find ourselves in a play of light and shadows and stone and bronze, among flowers, trees and the occasional insect. A reflecting pool and a platform for stage performances sit in the middle of the grounds. When camping, the hide is used as a mattress; at home, it’s clothing. Peter Mather Jeffrey Peter, of Old Crow, Yukon, cleans a caribou hide during an autumn hunt. When camping, the hide is used as a mattress; at home, it’s clothing. Peter Mather In the Gwich'in language, there’s a name for the area just north of the Brooks Range, the mountains that run along the northern rim of Alaska and divide the densely forested interior from the spare Arctic coast. Where the land flattens out into low-lying tundra before meeting the Beaufort Sea is Iizhik Gwats’an Gwandaii Goodlit , or “the sacred place where life begins.” The name honors the role this 1.5-million-acre swath of Arctic coastal plain plays as the primary calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou, a herd of more than 200,000 animals. This crucial habitat is where tens of thousands of pregnant cows migrate each year to give birth. Porcupine caribou, named for a river within their range, can trek 3,000 miles in a year to reach their calving grounds north of the Brooks Range. SCIENCE LAELAPS For the Love of Dinosaurs By Riley Black Published May 26, 2013 • 10 min read Last month, Scientific American/FSG Books was kind enough to publish my ode to dinosaurs and the science that is changing our perceptions of how they lived – My Beloved Brontosaurus . I wrote the following op-ed to accompany the book’s release, published here after failing to find a niche elsewhere. I was a little dinomaniac. I can’t recall exactly when the fever set in, but I ceaselessly pestered my parents to tape every movie and television show even remotely associated with the word “dinosaur”, my curiosity further fueled by museum trips, toys, and lavishly-illustrated books. I’ve still got the bug. Even now, I feel the same compulsion to chew on scattered dinosauriana, in both their scientific and pop culture garbs. But why? The inexorable pull of dinosaurs is a mystery. When I talk about dinosaurs to anyone who isn’t quite so enamored as I am, but remembers their own dinosaur phase or is suffering through that of their own children, they often ask why dinosaurs have such a persistent hold on pop culture and our imagination. Dinosaurs are seemingly everywhere, from lunchboxes and sports mascots to bleeding-edge scientific discoveries. In most cases, the U.S. branch of a foreign corporation or partnership is treated as a foreign person.
